paragraphs.text: People say that the dog is man's best friend. They say this because dogs are loyal and loving pets. Unfortunately, man is not always a good friend to dogs. This was the case with Patrasche and his master.

Patrasche was a beautiful, sandy-colored working dog from Flanders in Belgium. Dogs from Flanders were famous because they were so strong. They could pull heavy carts and work hard for hours, like small horses.

When Patrasche was still a puppy, he was sold to a merchant. His new master sold pots and pans for a living. He traveled all over Belgium with his cart of goods, from the blue sea to the green mountains.

Patrasche's master was a drunkard and a fat, mean man. He piled his cart high with pans, buckets, jars, brass tins, and cooking pots. Whenever Patrasche tired from the heavy load, his master beat him without mercy.

One day, Patrasche was pulling the cart along a straight, dusty road. They were heading to the lovely city of Antwerp, where the great painter Rubens once lived. The merchant walked lazily beside the cart, smoking a pipe.

It was the middle of summer and very warm. Patrasche's master stopped at every wine shop along the way. But poor Patrasche─his master never unhooked him from the cart or gave him a drink of water. Patrasche was exhausted, but he was a hardworking dog and kept walking. When he started to slow down, his master hit him with a whip.
"Patrasche, you stupid dog, go faster!" he yelled.
The whip stung Patrasche's side. His eyes were full of dust and his muscles ached.
"Lazy beast," yelled his master. "We must reach Antwerp tonight. There is a market there tomorrow."
Still Patrasche pulled with his tired legs, but the effort was too much. He staggered and fell over on his side. He lay in the middle of the dusty road, motionless in the full heat of the sun.
Patrasche's cruel master gave him his usual medicine─a kick in the ribs and a lash from his whip. Patrasche had received beatings many times before but this time he did not move or cry.
The merchant cursed Patrasche. "Get up, you lazy dog!" he shouted. "We've still got three miles to walk!"

But Patrasche did not hear him. He was too tired even to feel his master's blows. The merchant cursed the poor dog again. He kicked his body off the road and into the grass. Patrasche's master lifted the front of the cart. With a frown and a moan, he began to pull it down the road.

For two long, cruel years, Patrasche had worked for his master from morning to night. He had been loyal and strong. But the merchant had forgotten him already. Muttering to himself as he pulled his cart, the merchant left Patrasche to die.
"When I reach the next village, I'll steal the first dog I see wandering around," the merchant thought.
He kept walking and didn't look back. Poor Patrasche was too exhausted even to lift his head and moan.
Patrasche lay still in the grass ditch. His cruel master had left him and was now far away. The road was busy, and hundreds of people passed by. Some were on foot, and some rode horses.
Some people saw him, but most did not even look. No one stopped. A dead dog was not worth a thought.

After a while, a little old man who was bent and lame came by. A little boy walked with him. The old man looked at the dog with pity, and the little boy too. They knelt down beside the dog. With much effort, the old man lifted Patrasche out of the ditch. Then he and the boy carried Patrasche back home to their little hut.

The old man's name was Jehan. When Jehan had turned eighty, his daughter had died. He was asked to look after her two-year-old son. The old man could barely support himself, but he took the little boy willingly. Jehan's grandson was named Nello. They lived at the edge of a small village in a small but clean mud hut. They kept a little garden where they grew beans and pumpkins and herbs.
There were only two dozen houses in the village. Their walls were painted white and shone in the sun like snow. They had colorful red roofs and shutters of bright green or sky blue.

In the center of the village stood a red windmill. Around Jehan's hut stretched flat pastures and fields of corn. A great canal ran through the village and the fields. On both sides of the canal, long lines of poplar trees bent their branches in the breeze.

Across the fields, the distant town of Antwerp was just visible on the horizon. But the tall spire of the Antwerp cathedral stood out. It shone bright in the morning sun, and at dusk, its shadow stood out against the clouds.

Jehan and Nello made Patrasche a little straw bed in the corner of their hut. He was very weak, but still alive. For many days, Patrasche lay there, not moving. At night, Nello stayed awake, listening anxiously to his breathing. Jehan could not give Patrasche much food. He barely had enough for himself and his grandson. In his youth, Jehan had been a soldier. But his leg had been injured during the war. This made it difficult for him to work, and he had been poor ever since. Some days, Jehan and Nello had nothing to eat. But even though their lives were hard, they were content. Jehan was very gentle and good to the boy, and the boy was beautiful, truthful, and kind.

During Patrasche's long recovery, Nello and his grandfather grew very fond of him. Nello leaned his cheek against Patrasche's fur at night, and they both slept soundly. Patrasche became part of their little family.

One day, Patrasche made a noise, a little bark. Jehan and Nello laughed and then wept with joy. Little Nello made a necklace of flowers for Patrasche and hugged him around his huge neck. Patrasche was getting better.

A few weeks later, Patrasche's health and strength returned. He stood up, and his big brown eyes showed surprise. Nobody was hitting him or cursing him. He looked lovingly at Jehan and Nello. He owed them his life.

Old Jehan, little Nello, and Patrasche, the great working dog of Flanders, lived happily together. Their meals came from their little garden. They had only a little money, which Jehan earned by delivering milk. Every day, Jehan filled a little green cart with cans of milk from his neighbors. He pulled the cart to Antwerp, where he sold the milk. Jehan's neighbors knew he was an honest man. They happily let him deliver their milk and collect the money for them.
But it was becoming hard work for the old man. He was 83, and the town of Antwerp was three miles away. Nello was too little to help, and every day, the trip took Jehan longer and longer.

When Patrasche was well again, he watched Jehan load the milk cans onto his cart. Then he watched as Jehan started slowly down the road. The next morning, Patrasche jumped up from his straw bed. He went over to Jehan and pushed him happily with his nose.
"What are you doing, Patrasche?" the old man scolded playfully. "Come on, out of my way. I have to take this milk into town."

Patrasche walked over to the cart and barked. Patrasche placed himself between the cart's handles and stood patiently. He wanted to show Jehan that he could pull the cart. Although Jehan understood, he resisted Patrasche's idea. Jehan thought it was wrong to make dogs work like slaves. Jehan tried to shoo him away, but Patrasche was stubborn. He tried to pull the cart with his teeth and managed to move it a little. Then he stood patiently again, as if to say, "I am a strong dog, and I can help."
Eventually, Jehan smiled. "You are a very persistent dog," he said, patting him.
Jehan understood that Patrasche was grateful. He knew Patrasche wanted to repay him for everything he had done.

That evening, Jehan made a harness for Patrasche. After that, Patrasche dutifully pulled the cart every morning. The bells on his harness jingled as he walked. Whenever Jehan tried to help, Patrasche barked. It was as if he were saying, "It is my job, and I will do my duty."

Sadly, Jehan grew weaker. When the winter came, he was thankful for Patrasche's help. Snow and mud covered the road. Without Patrasche, he would not have been able to deliver the milk through the cold.

But for Patrasche, the work seemed like heaven. It was fun to pull the bright green cart with its shiny brass milk cans. No one whipped him. Instead, the kind old man walked beside him, often giving him a gentle pat.
Besides, Patrasche finished his work by early afternoon. Then he was free to do as he wished─to stretch, to sleep in the sun, to wander in the fields, or to play with other dogs.

Patrasche was happiest of all when he played with Nello. Nello and Patrasche were best friends. In fact, they were very similar. They were both orphans, and Jehan had looked after them both and saved their lives.

Since Patrasche first arrived at the little hut, the friendship between the boy and the dog had strengthened every day. They played together every afternoon and loved each other greatly. The big dog and little Nello were never long apart.
The next winter, the aches in Jehan's bones made it too difficult for him to move. He had been crippled for years. But now, it was impossible for him even to walk beside the cart.
Little Nello was now six years old. He knew Antwerp well because he had accompanied his grandfather there many times. So, Nello took Jehan's place beside the cart and walked with Patrasche instead.

Nello sold the milk in Antwerp and received the coins in exchange. He brought the money back to the farmers in the village. He did all his work with an innocent dignity; everyone who met him was charmed. Nello was a beautiful child, with tender eyes, a lovely face, and light blond hair. Often when Nello and Patrasche were walking into town, an artist stopped them on the road. He would ask little Nello if he could sketch him.

Since Nello and Patrasche were never in a rush, Nello usually agreed. Besides, Nello loved seeing the finished sketch. The artist would carefully draw Nello and Patrasche with the fields of Flanders in the background.

Nello and Patrasche delivered the milk so well that Jehan did not worry. On summer mornings, he sat in the sunlit doorway of the hut. He watched the happy pair head down the road. In the afternoon, he rested and then watched for their return. At the hut, Patrasche would shake himself free of his harness with a happy bark. Nello would proudly tell his grandfather everything they had done. Then they would all eat a dinner of rye bread and soup.

At the end of each day, the shadows grew long in the pastures. The distant spire of the great cathedral faded in the twilight. At night, Nello and Patrasche lay down together while the old man said a prayer.

So the days and the years went on. The lives of Nello and Patrasche were happy and innocent. Flanders is not a place of majestic beauty, but the land is green and wide. Its spacious horizons are pleasant and welcoming.
In summer, fall, and spring, little Nello and Patrasche would lie in the grass beside the canal. They watched the boats drift by and breathed the salty air of the sea.

In the winter, life was harder. They had to get up in the dark and the bitter cold. The hut was not much warmer than a shed, and the wind found many holes in the walls. The bare fields around the hut looked flat and grim. The cold pinched little Nello's hands and toes. The snow and ice cut the brave, tireless feet of Patrasche. But the two friends never complained. They walked over the frozen fields together, accompanied by the chime of the bells on Patrasche's harness.

Sometimes, in the streets of Antwerp, a housewife would bring them a bowl of soup and a handful of bread. Sometimes, a kindly merchant would throw a little firewood into the small cart as they went home.

Patrasche worked through the heat of summer and the chills of winter. Even though he was often hungry, he was grateful and content. As Patrasche worked, the eyes that he loved smiled down on him. It was enough.
There was only one thing that made Patrasche uneasy. It was this: Nello often left Patrasche alone in the street.
Antwerp, as all the world knows, is full of old churches. Nello loved to visit them.
Antwerp's churches are jammed in everywhere, in almost every alley and street. Its churches are quiet, grand, old places of the past. They are dark, ancient, and beautiful.

Many of the churches contain the art of Antwerp's most beloved citizen: the great painter Peter Paul Rubens. Rubens was born in Flanders in 1577 and grew up in Antwerp. By the age of twenty-one, he was already an excellent painter.

Rubens left Antwerp and, like other great painters of the time, he went to Italy. In Italy, he worked as a court painter and painted altars of churches in Rome. His works are famous for their color, their light, and their feeling of energy.

In 1608, Rubens returned to Antwerp, where he continued to paint for many years. His paintings have religious themes and decorate its many ancient churches. In one of Antwerp's churches lies Rubens' tomb. Without Rubens, what is Antwerp? Merely a dirty, bustling market city. But because Rubens lived and worked there, Antwerp is sacred. Both worshippers of God and lovers of art honor its soil.

Some afternoons, after Nello and Patrasche finished delivering the milk, Nello would stop outside a church. He would tell Patrasche to wait outside while he went in. Most often, he visited Antwerp's great cathedral. Once or twice, Patrasche tried to follow. He stepped through the cathedral's large gate, pulling his milk-cart behind, but a guard always sent him back. He waited on the street stones outside the iron gate and watched the people go by.
"What does Nello do inside?" wondered Patrasche. "Sometimes he is inside for more than one hour!"

Patrasche worried whenever Nello disappeared inside a church or went into the cathedral. Patrasche wasn't bothered just because Nello visited churches. Patrasche knew it was normal for people to go to church. After all, the farmers in their village went to the small gray church opposite the red windmill. Patrasche was worried because Nello always looked pale, when he came out.
Nello was usually a talkative boy. But whenever he visited the cathedral, he would stay silent for hours after.
If Nello visited the cathedral, when they returned home he never wanted to play. Instead, he would sit and gaze at the evening skies. Patrasche thought the little boy should not be so serious.

But Nello kept visiting the cathedral and the churches. Patrasche could do nothing except wait in the street. He stretched himself out on the stones, yawned, and sighed. When Nello came out of the cathedral, he always hugged Patrasche and kissed his forehead. In a soft voice, he would murmur, "If I could only see them, Patrasche!"
"See what?" wondered Patrasche.

One afternoon, Nello and Patrasche had finished delivering the milk, and once more, Patrasche was watching outside the gates of the cathedral. Patrasche noticed the church guard leave. He crept through the gates, up to the cathedral's open doors, and inside.

In the dark church, he saw Nello kneeling down and staring at the high altar. On it was the painting of the Assumption by Rubens. On the walls of the cathedral, on either side of the altar, were two more paintings. But each was covered by a curtain. Patrasche saw two wealthy gentlemen put money in a metal box. Then, they went behind the curtain to see one of the paintings.
Nello noticed Patrasche, went over to him, and took him gently outside. He looked back at the veiled paintings as they left. His face was wet with tears.

"It's terrible I can't see them, Patrasche," he said, "just because I'm poor! I'm sure Rubens thought everybody should see his paintings!" Nello said. "But those two paintings are behind curtains! No one sees them except rich people. If I could only see them, I would die a happy person."
It was true that Nello's little family was poor. Any extra money was used to buy firewood or more food. Nello longed to see the two veiled paintings, and Patrasche knew he could do nothing to help.

The little boy loved art. When Nello stood before the altar painting in Antwerp's cathedral, he felt as if he were in heaven. The glory of the great master's art made his heart stir with joy. Nello drew with whatever he could find. He drew on street stones with chalk or with charcoal on a scrap of wood. He drew the cathedral spire at sunset and the morning mist on the fields, whatever he saw around him. Because Nello lived in poverty, he did not go to school. Nobody paid him much attention, except Jehan and Patrasche. But not even they─not even Nello himself─realized that the boy was a genius at art.
Many times from his bed at night, Jehan would say, "Nello, when you grow up, I hope you'll own this hut and the garden, and be called 'master' by your neighbors."
The old soldier had wandered over all the earth in his youth and gained nothing. He thought that the best fate for his grandson would be to live, grow old, and die in the same home.

Nello dreamed of other things besides being a farmer and being respected by his neighbors. He said nothing to his grandfather, but as he drew the beauty around him, he dreamed of becoming an artist. Nello whispered his dreams to Patrasche when they walked into town at daybreak every morning. Patrasche looked up at Nello with loving eyes. He hoped Nello's dreams would come true. Besides Patrasche, Nello had only one other friend. She was pretty, little Alois Cogez, who lived at the old red mill. Aside from the loyal Patrasche, she was the only one who knew his dream.

When Nello was fifteen years old, he, Jehan, and Patrasche still lived together happily in their little hut. Life had not changed. Nello and Patrasche delivered the milk daily. Nello still dreamed of being an artist and drew pictures every day.
On one fine day, Nello and Patrasche had finished their work. As usual, they went to find Nello's friend Alois to play. She was Nello's best friend, and they had played together for many years.

Alois was twelve. She had no brothers or sisters. Her father, the miller, was the richest man in the village. Her little dresses were always pretty. Her cheeks were rosy, and her sweet, dark eyes shone. Many families wanted their sons to marry her when she was older. But Alois had no interest in older boys. She just loved playing with her friend Nello and his great, friendly dog.

First, Alois, Nello, and Patrasche went up to the old, gray church together. Then they raced to the fields and played hide-and-seek in the long cornflowers. Later they lay down, exhausted. Alois took a little nap, and Patrasche laid his head in her lap. Nello found a clean piece of pine wood and took out a stick of charcoal. He started to draw a small portrait of Alois and Patrasche. Nello drew quickly and confidently. He drew Alois' dark hair falling on her bright cheeks. He drew Patrasche's golden fur shining in the sun. Behind them, a patch of flowers tilted in the breeze.

Alois' father, the miller, came walking into the field. He was a good man, but was a strict father. When he saw the portrait, tears came to his eyes. It captured his daughter's likeness perfectly. It was beautiful. The miller told Alois to go home.
"Your mother wants you," he said.
"But Daddy, I'm having fun!" Alois protested.
"Obey your father," the miller said roughly.
The miller snatched the wood from Nello's hands and looked at it closely.
"Do you make drawings of my daughter a lot?" he asked. His voice trembled.
Nello blushed and hung his head.
"I draw everything I see," he murmured.
The miller was silent. He thought about Nello and his life of poverty. Then the miller held out a coin.
"Drawing is a foolish pastime," he said. "But the picture is like Alois. It will please her mother. Take this coin and I will take the picture."
Nello stopped blushing. He lifted his head and put his hands behind his back.
"Keep the money and keep the portrait, Master Cogez," he said simply. "You have often been good to me."
Then Nello called Patrasche. Together they walked home across the field.
"With that coin, I might have seen the master's paintings," he said to Patrasche. "But I could not sell her picture─not even for them."
The miller walked back from the fields to his mill.
"That little boy Nello should not spend so much time with Alois," he said to his wife that night. "There may be trouble later. He is fifteen years old, and she is twelve."
"He is also a handsome young man," said his wife. "He is a good boy too."
She looked at the portrait of Alois that Nello had drawn. It was hanging on the wall next to the wooden cuckoo clock.
"Then, if they ever fell in love," said the wife, "would it matter? She is rich enough for both of them. Happiness is the most important thing!"

"That's a foolish thing to say!" said the miller, slamming his pipe on the table. "The boy is almost a beggar. If he becomes a painter, he'll be worse than a beggar. Promise me that Nello and Alois will not play together again!"

The miller's wife could not bear to separate them completely. Even so, they were kept apart in many little ways. After church, Nello wasn't permitted to talk with Alois. And in the afternoons, her parents kept her busy with chores.
Nello was a proud and sensitive boy. He realized what was happening and was hurt. So, Nello and Patrasche no longer went to the mill to visit Alois.
"Why can't I see my friend Alois?" Nello thought. "I haven't done anything wrong!"
He wondered if he had angered the miller that day in the fields. He did not know that his only sin was being poor.
Sometimes, Nello and Alois ran into each other. When that happened, he held her hand and told her to go home.
"Sorry, Alois, but your father will be angry. He thinks that I make you idle. You must go." Nello said this with a sad heart.
Without Alois, the earth did not look as bright as it used to. But Nello did not complain.
As his grandfather said, "We are poor and must take what God sends. The poor cannot choose."

One day, little Alois found Nello walking near the canal. She ran up to him, crying. Tomorrow was her birthday, but she was not allowed to invite him to her party. In other years, Nello had always been at her birthday party. Nello kissed her on the cheek and asked her to stop crying.
He told her, "It will be different one day, Alois. One day, that little portrait your father has will be worth a lot of money."
"Then your father will invite me in again," Nello said. "Just remember me always, dear little Alois. If you do, I promise that, one day, I will be a great artist."
"And if I forget you?" the pretty child asked, pouting a little.
Nello's eyes left her face and wandered to the distant horizon. There was a smile on his face both sweet and sad.
"I will be great still," he said under his breath. "I will be great still, or die, Alois."
The next evening, Nello sat at the door of the hut with Patrasche. He heard the sounds of Alois' birthday celebrations.
"Never mind, Patrasche," he said, with his arms around the dog's neck. "It will all be different one day."

Nello and Patrasche sat at the door of the hut. Across the village from the mill, Nello could hear the sounds of Alois' birthday. Little Alois was Nello's best friend, but her father had refused to invite him to her party. Nello was sad, but he turned his mind to other things. He looked at the little shed behind the hut. No one, except him, went in there, and inside was his great secret.

Nello's secret was an easel. He had made it himself with pieces of wood. A large sheet of paper was attached to the easel. On the paper was a picture of an old man sitting on a fallen tree. The old man was Michel, the woodman. Nello had seen Michel many times, sitting alone on a log at dusk. The portrait was simple. It had a few small flaws, if you wanted to look for them. Yet it was very real and very beautiful.

Nello had another secret: he planned to enter this portrait in an art competition. The competition was in Antwerp. It was open to anyone under eighteen years old. The prize was two hundred francs. All spring, summer, and autumn, Nello worked on his portrait of the woodman. When his milk deliveries were finished for the day, he crept into the shed to draw. He drew with charcoal, and many times, he went without food so that he could buy more charcoal.
Nello said nothing to anyone. His grandfather would not have understood, and he did not see Alois anymore. He told only Patrasche.
He whispered in the dog's ear, "The artist Rubens would give me first prize if he were the judge!"
Patrasche agreed. Patrasche knew that Rubens had loved dogs because he had painted them so well.
"People who love dogs are always good," Patrasche reasoned.
The competition deadline was the first day of December. The prizes were to be announced on December 24 so that the winner could celebrate on Christmas Day.

November 30, the day before the deadline, was a cold winter day. At twilight, Nello put his picture in the green milk cart. With Patrasche's help, they walked to Antwerp and through its dark streets. They found the large public building where the competition was being held.
Nello nervously walked inside and set his picture on the table provided.
"Perhaps it is worth nothing at all. How can I tell?" he thought.
As Nello walked away, his heart beat fast. "Maybe it's a foolish idea," he thought. "I am just a poor boy who can barely read! Could I draw anything that a real artist might admire?"

Nello and Patrasche passed the cathedral. There, Nello thought he saw the figure of Rubens in the fog. The figure seemed to say, "Have courage! I had to be brave to be a great painter. You can be too!"
Nello ran home through the cold night, comforted. He had done his best, and he knew this was all he could do. Nello fell asleep, and Patrasche curled up next to him.

It was December, and the winter was quite bad already. The night after Patrasche and Nello had returned from town, snow fell. It fell for many days after that. The paths in the fields disappeared, and all the streams froze. The sun rose late these mornings.

Nello and Patrasche's work became harder. They woke up in the cold. They carried the milk to the silent town in darkness. It was hard work, especially for Patrasche. He was older now, and his joints were stiff and his bones often ached. But he would not give up his share of the work.

Nello would have pulled the cart himself, but Patrasche would not allow it. Patrasche accepted only the smallest offers of help. Sometimes, he let Nello give the cart a push if it was stuck in the ice.
"Take a rest today, Patrasche!" Nello would say in the morning. "I can pull the cart by myself."
But Patrasche would not listen. Every day, he would bring Nello his harness; every day, he would walk steadily through the snow.
"One must never rest until one dies," thought Patrasche.
Sometimes, he thought that the end of his days was not far off. His sight was growing dim, and his bones hurt when he got up in the morning.
"Poor Patrasche, we shall soon lie quiet together, you and I," said Jehan one night.
He stroked Patrasche's head with his old hand, and Patrasche licked his cheek with love.
But both of them wondered, "When we are gone, who will care for Nello?"

One December afternoon, Patrasche and Nello were walking back from Antwerp. The snow had become as hard as rock over the roads and fields. On the road, they found a pretty little puppet. The puppet was beautiful. Its costume was made of red and gold silk, and its face was made from wood. Even though it lay on the road, it was clean and wasn't broken.

Nello picked it up, thinking to find its owner. He stopped people passing by, but no one knew who the puppet belonged to. It was a busy road. Many merchants and farmers traveled it, and the puppet could have been lost by anyone. After several hours of stopping and asking people, Nello had no success. So he decided to give the puppet to Alois. He knew that she loved playing with puppets and dolls.

Alois' father would not allow Nello to visit their house, but Nello had an idea. He would pass the puppet to her through her window. He would do it at night when nobody would see. He crept quietly up to the miller's house, looking carefully around. The light was on in Alois' room, and he tapped quietly on the glass.
Alois opened the window and looked out, a little frightened. Nello put the puppet into her hands.
"Here is a doll I found in the snow, Alois. Take it," he whispered. "I must go before anyone sees. Good-bye!" said Nello.
Before Alois had time to thank him, he ran off. But the miller, who had heard a noise outside, opened the front door and saw Nello hurrying away in the dark.

The same night that Nello had visited Alois at her window, there was a fire at the mill. The fire engines came from Antwerp, rushing through the snow. Many villagers also came to help. Nello, too, came to save the mill from burning. The outer buildings and many cornfields were destroyed. Thankfully, the mill itself and the house were unharmed. The miller was insured and would lose nothing. Nevertheless, he was furious.
The miller declared that the fire was not an accident. He insisted that someone had set fire to the mill.
When he saw Nello helping put out the fire, he said, "I saw you here in the night. I think you know something about the fire!" Nello listened to Master Cogez. He was too shocked to reply.
"How could anyone say such a thing except as a joke?" Nello thought. But clearly, the miller was not joking.

The next day, the miller told his neighbors that he suspected Nello. People in the village gossiped. They said Nello was angry with the miller because he was not allowed to see Alois. In their hearts, the villagers didn't really believe that Nello had lit the fire. But the miller was powerful, and the villagers were poor. They didn't dare question the miller's opinion. So the villagers no longer smiled at Nello or said hello. When Nello and Patrasche picked up their milk, the villagers just looked at the ground. Nello could do nothing.

"You are very cruel to Nello," the miller's wife said to her husband. "He is innocent. Maybe Nello was upset that he couldn't see Alois anymore. But he is a good boy. He would never set fire to our house."
When he thought over his wife's words, the miller felt she was right. But the miller was a stubborn man. Once he had said something, he would not change his mind.
Nello, for his part, never complained about the miller. To Patrasche only, he sighed a little about what had happened.

But then he thought, "If my picture wins, he'll be sorry, perhaps." Still, it was a difficult time for the 15-year-old boy. He had done nothing wrong, and he was a good young man. Yet it seemed as if the whole world were against him.
Winters in Flanders are hard. In the village, there was a lot of snow and little food. Usually, the villagers helped each other out, but this winter was different.

No one came to visit Nello's grandfather or left extra milk at their door. And then, it got worse. A man from Antwerp started to deliver milk with a large wagon and a mule. Most villagers stopped giving their milk to Nello to deliver. Instead of twenty customers, now Nello had only four.

Patrasche did not understand the change. In the mornings, he would stop, as always, at all the familiar gates. Now the gates stayed closed. Patrasche had less milk to carry in the green cart, and Nello had fewer coins in his pocket.

At Christmas, the little village was cheerful. The weather was wild and cold. The snow was six feet deep and frozen hard. Despite all, the villagers smiled and were happy. Bells jingled on horses in the street. Every house in the village was decorated for Christmas. Cakes and candy were given as gifts. Friends gathered in homes for joking and dancing. Pots full of soup sat on the stoves.

It was dark and sad only in the little hut. A week before Christmas, Death entered the tiny home. Jehan, Nello's loving grandfather and Patrasche's caring owner, passed away. Nello and Pastrasche were left utterly alone. Jehan had been sick for a long time, spending his days in bed. He hadn't spoken for many weeks, but he had always smiled for Nello and Patrasche. His loss gave them both great grief.
Nello and Patrasche stayed with Jehan's body all day in the hut. The next afternoon, his coffin was taken to an unmarked grave by the little gray church. Nello and Patrasche were the only mourners.
The miller's wife saw Nello and Patrasche walking behind the coffin on the way to the church.
"Surely, my husband will change his mind about Nello. He will let Nello see Alois," she thought, looking at Master Cogez.
The miller knew her thought, but he would not change his mind.
"The boy is a beggar," he said to himself. "He should not be friends with Alois."

The miller's wife did not dare say anything aloud. But after Nello and Patrasche had left the grave, she put some flowers into Alois' hands. She told Alois to take the flowers and place them on Jehan's grave.

Nello and Patrasche went home with broken hearts. When they got home, a small note was nailed to the door. Nello read it. It said the rent for the little hut was overdue. The owner of the hut was a farmer and also a friend of Master Cogez. Nello slowly walked down the road to the farmer's house. After he had paid for the funeral, Nello had no money left.

The farmer answered the door with an annoyed look on his face. He listened to Nello explain his situation. The farmer's look did not change. He told Nello he wanted everything in the hut as payment for the rent ─ every pot and pan. Then the farmer told Nello and Patrasche to be out of the hut by the next day. Nello begged the farmer to change his mind, but he wouldn't listen. The farmer began to shout, and Nello turned with Patrasche to leave.
The hut was only a simple home, but they had been happy there. In the summer, the hut was pretty and bright. The garden had given them vegetables. In the shed, Nello had drawn his pictures.
All night long, the boy and the dog sat in the hut, without a fire to keep them warm. They slept close together. Nello and Patrasche had nothing left but each other.
It was the morning of Christmas Eve. Nello woke up and shivered. It was freezing inside the little hut. Nello held onto his closest friend, and his tears dropped onto the great dog's forehead.

"Let's go, Patrasche," Nello murmured. "We won't wait to be kicked out." They stepped outside into the cold. Patrasche hung his head as he passed the little green cart. It didn't belong to him anymore. The farmer who owned the hut was taking it for the rent. He was taking everything else in the hut too.

Nello and Patrasche walked the long road into Antwerp. It was the same road they had walked to deliver milk every day. It was still early morning. The windows were closed on most of the houses along the road. In a few houses, people were awake.
At one house, the door stood open a little. Inside, an old woman was cooking breakfast. Nello's grandfather, Jehan, had been kind to her many times.
"Do you have any leftovers for Patrasche?" Nello called timidly from the door. "He's old, and he's eaten nothing since yesterday."
The old woman shut the door quickly, murmuring about the high price of flour.
Nello and Patrasche kept walking. They didn't stop at any more houses. It was ten o'clock in the morning when they reached Antwerp.
"I wish I had something I could sell, so I could buy some bread for Patrasche," thought Nello.

But Nello had nothing, except the clothes he wore and his wooden shoes. Somehow Patrasche understood. He knew that Nello longed to ease his hunger and aches. He put his nose into Nello's hand. "Please, don't worry about me," he seemed to say.

The winner of the art competition was to be announced at noon. Nello and Patrasche walked toward the public building in the middle of town. There, many young people crowded the steps and waited in the street. Some boys were older than Nello, and some were younger. All of them were with parents or friends. Nello's heart was sick with fear as he found an empty place on the steps. He held Patrasche close.

At noon, the great bells of Antwerp's City Hall rang loudly. The doors at the top of the stairs opened. The crowd rushed forward. The winning picture would be displayed high on a wall inside the entrance.
Nello looked up, but he couldn't see. Too many people were in the way. Everyone was stretching and pushing to see the winning picture.
At last the crowd thinned and he saw it! It was not his. Nello felt dizzy. With Patrasche's help, he staggered outside. "It's all over, Patrasche," Nello murmured. "All over."

They both felt weak from lack of food, and walked slowly back to the village. Snow was starting to fall, and a storm was coming. It was four o'clock when they reached the village. Suddenly, Patrasche stopped. He smelled something in the snow. He pushed his nose into the snow and picked up a small leather bag with his teeth. Patrasche gave the bag to Nello. Nello looked at it closely. The name on the bag said Master Cogez. Inside was two thousand francs ─ enough to buy a small farm!

Nello held the leather bag in his hand. He had never seen so much money before. He put the bag in his shirt and patted Patrasche on the head. Nello walked straight toward the mill. He knocked on the front door. The miller's wife opened the door. Alois stood behind her. Both looked very upset.
"What is it, Nello?" Alois asked. "Go before my father sees you!"
"Master Cogez is in a terrible mood tonight," the miller's wife said. "He dropped some money and, in this snow, he will never find it. It was all our savings," she sobbed.
Nello stepped inside and gave the leather bag to the miller's wife. He called Patrasche into the house.

"Patrasche found the money in the snow," Nello said. "Tell Master Cogez to please look after Patrasche. I can't take care of him anymore." Nello bent down to kiss Patrasche good-bye. Then he quickly closed the door and disappeared into the night. The miller's wife and daughter were speechless. Patrasche went to the door and whined. He wanted to follow Nello, but the door was closed.

Alois and her mother tried to comfort Patrasche. They brought him milk and a big bone. They gave him a blanket to lie on near the warm fire. Nothing worked. Patrasche sat stubbornly by the door and would not move.
At six o'clock the miller came home. He looked very tired and his face was sad.
"The money is lost forever," he said. "I took a lantern and looked everywhere, but it's gone. Some of that money was for Alois' future. I'm so sorry, Alois."
His wife put the money into his hands and told him the story. The miller walked to a chair by the fire. He sat down and covered his face, ashamed.
"I have been cruel to the boy," he muttered. "I don't deserve his goodness."
Little Alois crept close to her father. "Can Nello come here again, Father?" she whispered bravely. "Can he come and play tomorrow, like he used to?"
The miller hugged his daughter tightly. His lips trembled with emotion.
"Yes, of course Nello can play with you," the miller said. "He can come here on Christmas Day, and any day of the year. I have treated Nello very badly. I must make it up to him."
Little Alois kissed her father with joy. She ran to where Patrasche sat by the door. Patrasche was still waiting and hoping that Nello would return. They had never spent a night apart.
"And tonight may I give Patrasche lots of food?" she asked, giving the dog a hug.
Her father looked at her. The stubbornness had washed from his face.
"Yes, yes. Let the dog have the best food," he said.
The miller sat with his head in his hand and was quiet for a long time. He thought about his actions over and over. Nello was only fifteen years old and had nothing.
"Even so," the miller thought, "he is a better man than me."

Outside, the night was dark, but inside the miller's house logs burned in the fireplace. Delicious smells filled the kitchen: roast ham, bread, honey, and cookies. Evergreen branches hung from the rafters, and holly hung on the wall. It was Christmas Eve. Some neighbors came in for a glass of wine and a slice of ham. They shook the miller's hand and laughed with his wife. Alois was happy too. She looked forward to seeing Nello tomorrow, on Christmas Day.

Alois put out a big bowl of meat for Patrasche, but he didn't move. Patrasche's loyalty to Nello was too strong. He was hungry and cold, but without Nello, he would not eat. Patrasche had not moved from the door since Nello had left. He was waiting until he could escape.
"The dog wants Nello," said Master Cogez. "Good dog! In the morning, I will go over to the hut to see Nello."
But only Patrasche knew that Nello was not in the hut. Only Patrasche knew that Nello had no food or blankets. And only Patrasche knew that Nello was somewhere, out there, in the freezing cold.

Another neighbor arrived to join in the Christmas celebrations. When the neighbor did not close the door properly, Patrasche saw his chance. He quietly pushed the door open with his nose and ran out into the night. It was late. Snow had been falling all evening, and Nello's footprints were gone. It took Patrasche a long time to find Nello's scent. He ran back and forth, up and down the road, with his nose lowered to the snow.

When Patrasche found Nello's scent, he quickly followed it down the road. The weather was wild. The roads were sheets of ice, everything was dark, and the snow kept falling thick and fast. In the wind and darkness, Patrasche lost the scent. He stopped and circled around and around until he found it again. This happened over and over, but Patrasche wouldn't give up. Patrasche followed Nello's trail along the familiar road into Antwerp. It was past midnight when the dog arrived in the city. The streets were very dark. Sometimes a narrow ray of light shone through a wooden shutter, but that was all.

There was no sound except for the wind. Gusts roared down the narrow streets. The wooden shop signs banged against the walls, and the streetlamps shook. Many people had walked through the city streets that night. Friends had visited each other and families had gone to church. With so many scents to follow, it was difficult for Patrasche to find Nello's trail. Patrasche followed Nello's scent down twisting alleys and streets. He poked his nose into dark corners and doorways. Where was Nello? Would Patrasche ever find him on this dark, cold Christmas Eve?
Patrasche's fur was wet with snow. He shivered with cold. Finally, he followed Nello's scent to a familiar place─the Antwerp cathedral.
"Nello has gone to the things he loves," Patrasche thought.

Patrasche stopped at the gates of the cathedral. He had waited here many times while Nello gazed at the beautiful paintings inside. The tall gates had been blown open by the wind. Patrasche crept through the gates and up to the cathedral doors. It was long after midnight, and the huge wooden doors were closed. The Christmas Eve worshippers who had gone to midnight mass had gone home. Patrasche tried to push open one of the tall doors. It was locked. He tried another one. It was shut too.

He walked around the side of the cathedral. There he found a door someone had forgotten to lock, and he pushed his way inside. The cathedral was almost empty. As Patrasche walked along the stone floor, snow fell from his fur. He left a little trail of snow behind him. Patrasche saw a figure lying in front of the altar. It was Nello.

Patrasche crept up and put his paw on Nello's head. Nello cried out softly and grabbed Patrasche gently. "Let us lie down and die together," he murmured. "No one needs us, and we are all alone." Patrasche put his head upon the young boy's chest. There were great tears in the dog's sad brown eyes. The two friends lay close together in the freezing air. The cathedral's stone floor was as cold as snow.
They fell asleep, and together they dreamed. They dreamed of happier days─when they chased each other through the fields, played with little Alois, or watched boats sail on the canal.

Suddenly, pale rays of white light broke through the darkness. It was the moon. The snow had stopped falling and the clouds had slipped away. The moon's light shone through the high windows in the cathedral's arches.

Rubens' great paintings looked down on the still bodies on the stone floor. Curtains usually covered the two pictures on either side of the altar. When Nello had first entered in the dark, he had pulled the curtains aside. The two paintings were Rubens' The Elevation of the Cross and The Descent from the Cross. For one moment, they were both visible in the moonlight. Nello stood up. He stared at the paintings with joy and awe. Tears fell from his eyes. He cried out, "I have seen them at last! It is enough!" He fell back down and pulled himself close to Patrasche. They lay together again. The next morning, they were dead.
In the morning, a crowd gathered around their still forms. The miller was there. "I was cruel to him," he wept. "He should have been my son."
Little Alois sobbed bitterly. She stroked Nello's forehead. "Today was our playday," she said sadly.

A stranger arrived at the cathedral. "I am looking for the boy who did this drawing!" he said. He was a famous artist, and he held Nello's picture in his hand. "This should be the winning picture," he insisted, "and I want to teach this young man."

But it was too late. Nello and Patrasche, who had spent their lives together, had died together. Nello's arms hugged Patrasche's body tightly, so the villagers buried them together too. The little boy and the dog of Flanders, loyal and loving to the end!
